- 26,32: p→g
- 26,35: g→S
- 26,38: S→g

So the row shifted right by 3 (one block position): c17 took c20's value (b), c23 took c20's? Wait: new c23 = w = old c26? Old c26=w. New c26=S=old c29. New c29=p=old c32. New c32=g=old c35. New c35=S=old c38. New c38=g=old c41. New c44=w=old c17!
So: the top row of the band rotated right (toward the c44 side) by one step, and c17 wrapped around to c44. c20 and c41 weren't in my sample (I was sampling c in range(17,45,3) → 17,20,23,...,44 — wait, range(17,45,3) = 17,20,23,26,29,32,35,38,41,44. But the diff only shows 8 entries: 26,17 / 26,23 / 26,26 / 26,29 / 26,32 / 26,35 / 26,38 / 26,44. c20 and c41 are missing → their values didn't change?? If the row rotated right by one step, c20 should take old c17 (w), and c41 should take old c44 (g). But the diff doesn't show changes at 26,20 or 26,41...
Hmm, wait, maybe c20 and c41 weren't in the `before` dict? The pos list: for c in range(17,45,3): pos.append((26,c)) → 17,20,23,26,29,32,35,38,41,44. All included. So before[26,20] existed. If it changed, it should appear in the diff. It didn't → c20 is unchanged, c41 also unchanged.
So the rotation isn't a simple full-row shift. Let me recompute: new values: c17=b (old c20=b ✓), c23=w (old c26=w ✓), c26=S (old c29 ✓), c29=p (old c32 ✓), c32=g (old c35 ✓), c35=S (old c38 ✓), c38=g (old c41 ✓), c44=w (old c17 ✓). c20: old w; if the pattern continues, new c20 should be old c17 = w → no change (w→w, invisible in diff!). c41: old g; new should be old c44 = g → no change (g→g, invisible!).
So indeed: the entire top row of the band (10 blocks, c17..c44) rotated right by one step (toward c44), with wraparound: c44←c17. The unchanged c20/c41 were coincidental (same color).
So: clicking the top red piece rotates the top row of the band rightward (left→right, with wraparound). This is a 10-position cycle: c17→c20→...→c44→c17? Wait, direction: new c17 = old c20 means the block at c20 moved to c17 → blocks move left (toward c17)? Let me think: if the block at position c20 is now at c17, then the block moved from c20 to c17 = leftward (toward the red piece). And new c44 = old c17: the block at c17 moved to c44?? That's a jump, not a shift.
Hmm, contradiction: new c17=old c20 (shift left) and new c44=old c17 (c17→c44). If it's a leftward shift with wraparound, then new c17 should be old c44 (wrap), not old c20.
Let me redo this carefully. Old row (c17..c44): [w, b, b, w, S, p, g, S, g, g].
New row: c17=b, c20=w?, c23=w, c26=S, c29=p, c32=g, c35=S, c38=g, c41=g?, c44=w.
Assuming c20 and c41 are unchanged (w and g): new = [b, w, w, S, p, g, S, g, g, w].
Compare old=[w,b,b,w,S,p,g,S,g,g] with new=[b,w,w,S,p,g,S,g,g,w].
new[0]=b=old[1]; new[1]=w=old[3]? old[1]=b, old[3]=w. new[1]=w=old[3]. Hmm, new[2]=w=old[3]=w? new[3]=S=old[4]. new[4]=p=old[5]. new[5]=g=old[6]. new[6]=S=old[7]. new[7]=g=old[8]. new[8]=g=old[8]?? old[8]=g, old[9]=g. new[9]=w=old[0].
So new[i] = old[i+1] (for i=0..7), new[8]=old[8] (ambiguous, g), new[9]=old[0]. This is a leftward shift (blocks move from c20 to c17, i.e., toward the red piece), with wraparound: old c17 → new c44. So the cycle is: c17→c44→c41→...→c20→c17? No wait: the block at c17 moved to c44; the block at c20 moved to c17; the block at c23 moved to c20... So each block moves one step left (toward smaller c), and the block at the left end (c17) wraps to the right end (c44). So the cycle order (direction of motion): c20→c17→c44→c41→c38→...→c23→c20. That is, blocks circulate: left end → right end (jump), then right to left.
Equivalently, the row is a cycle in the order [c17, c20, c23, ..., c44], and blocks move one step in the direction of increasing index? Block at c20 (index 1) → c17 (index 0): index decreases. Block at c17 (index 0) → c44 (index 9): wraps. So blocks move in the direction of decreasing index, with wraparound. OK.
So clicking the top red piece = the top row of the band rotates one step "leftward" (toward the red piece), with wraparound.
Now, what about the bottom row (r35)? Probably clicking the bottom red piece rotates the bottom row. And the outer loop? Maybe clicking the green piece rotates the outer loop? Or maybe the outer loop doesn't rotate at all in this level — the Y block on the outer loop is... hmm, but the targets (26,35) and (35,35) are on the band rows! (26,35) is on the top row of the band (c35 is one of the 10 positions). (35,35) is on the bottom row of the band.
And the band has no Y... but wait, the targets are on the band rows, and the band rotates. The Y block is on the outer loop. If the outer loop also rotates (via the green piece?), the Y could move to (26,35)/(35,35)... but those positions are on the outer loop too (c35 column). Hmm, but if the band rows rotate independently, then the block at (26,35) belongs to the band, and the outer loop's c35 column is...
Ugh, the shared-position problem. Let me reconsider: maybe the outer "loop" isn't a loop. Maybe the top row r17 + c23/c35 (r20-23) + the band's top row r26 form one ring: a 5-wide, 3-row-tall ring? Positions: r17: c23,26,29,32,35 (5); c23: r20,23 (2); c35: r20,23 (2); r26: c23,26,29,32,35 (5). Total 14. But the band's top row also includes c17,20,38,41,44 (5 more), and those rotated with the top red click...
Wait, in the probe, the entire r26 row (c17..c44) rotated. So the band's top row is a single 10-cycle. And the r17 row didn't change. So the top red click only affects the r26 cycle.
Now the question is: does the outer loop (r17 row, c23/c35 columns, r44 row) rotate at all? If so, what controls it? The green piece? Let me probe the green piece.
Also, the bottom red piece probably rotates the r35 row.
But the key point: the targets (26,35) and (35,35) are on the band rows. The band has no Y block. So how can Y reach the targets? Unless the outer loop's Y can transfer to the band at the shared positions... or unless the required color at the targets isn't Y!
Hmm, wait. Let me look at the image again. The Y-dot markers surround (26,35) and (35,35). Currently (26,35)=S (after the probe), (35,35)=p.
Maybe the goal is: make the blocks at the marked positions the same color as each other? Or make them match the color of the small dots (Y)?
Or maybe the goal is: the marked positions are "gates" — when the correct color arrives, the level is cleared. In level 1, the marked corner needed Y. Here the markers are Y dots → probably Y is needed at both marked positions.
For Y to reach (26,35) or (35,35): the Y block is on the outer loop (17,32) and (38,23). If the outer loop rotates, Y can pass through (26,35) and (35,35) (both on the outer loop's c35 column). But if the band rows also rotate, the block at (26,35) is... which object is at (26,35)? After the band's top row rotated, (26,35) now holds S (which came from old c38). So the band's top row owns (26,35). The outer loop's c35 column also includes (26,35) — a conflict.
Maybe... the outer loop isn't a loop at all! Maybe the outer structure is two separate "arms": the top arm (r17 row + c23 r20-23 + c35 r20-23) connects to the band at (26,23) and (26,35); the bottom arm (r44 row + c23 r38-41 + c35 r38-41) connects at (35,23) and (35,35). And the arms rotate as a cycle: r17 row → c35 down → r26? No...
Let me probe: click the green piece (top right, (26,48)) and see what moves. Also click the bottom red (35,14). Two probes. Budget: the left strip is 64px, 5px per action → 12 actions; 1 used. 11 remaining. Probes: 2 more. Then the solution.
Actually, let me think about what the solution could be, to guide the probes.
If the goal is Y at both (26,35) and (35,35):
- Y1 is at (17,32) on the top arm. To reach (26,35): if the top arm is a cycle r17c23→r17c26→r17c29→r17c32→r17c35→r20c35→r23c35→r26c35 (target A) — 4 steps clockwise.
- Y2 is at (38,23) on the bottom arm. To reach (35,35): the bottom arm's cycle: r44c23→r41c23→r38c23→r35c23→r35c26→r35c29→r35c32→r35c35 (target B) — 6 steps. But wait, r35c23..c35 is the band's bottom row, which rotates with the bottom red! Conflict again.
Hmm, the shared positions keep being a problem. Unless the arms are: top arm = r17 (c23-35) + c23 (r20,23) + c35 (r20,23) + r26 (c23,26,29,32,35)?? That's a 14-cycle including 5 of the band's top row positions. But the probe showed the entire 10-band row rotating, including c23..c35. So no.
OK, let me step back. Maybe the outer loop doesn't rotate at all. The Y block is static decoration (like the small N piece at the top right (16-19,38-40) and the R piece at the top left (16-19,19-21)). The actual puzzle: two band rows (10-cycles each), controlled by the two red pieces (top red → top row leftward; bottom red → bottom row probably leftward). The targets (26,35) and (35,35) are on the band rows. The required color is... the Y dots suggest Y, but the band has no Y!
Band top row colors: w b b w S p g S g g. Band bottom row: w S b w b S p b g S. No Y. So Y can't be the required color (unless it comes from the outer loop).
Maybe the required color isn't Y. The Y dots might just be "target markers" (the color is arbitrary). What's the goal then? Possibilities:
1. Make both marked positions the same color.
2. Make the marked positions match a specific color (e.g., matching the color of the R/N pieces? R at top left, N at top right...).
3. Make each marked position match the color of the piece on the same row (red on the left → R? no R in the band).
4. The marked positions should be the same color as the block diagonally opposite / symmetrically placed.
5. The goal is to make the two band rows identical (as sequences)?
6. The goal: the marked positions should be S (sky)? Or match the color of the dots...
Hmm. Let me look at the markers again: the 1px Y dots at (25,34),(25,37),(28,34),(28,37) surround (26,35)-(27,36). In level 1, the markers were 2×2 Y blocks at the four corners of the target, and the target needed a Y block. Here the markers are 1px Y dots at the four corners of the target. Consistent: the target needs Y.
So Y must reach (26,35) and (35,35). The only Y blocks are on the outer loop. So the outer loop must rotate and transfer Y to the band at the shared positions?? That doesn't make sense mechanically...
Unless the outer loop and the band are actually one big cycle! Let me reconsider: maybe the entire structure is one loop:
Start from (26,17) → right along r26 to (26,44) → up? No, c44 has nothing above r26.
Or: (26,44) → ... hmm.
What about this loop: r26 row (c17→c44), then up c35? No, c44 is the right end.
Let me try: the loop is: r17 (c23→c35) → c35 (r20→r26) → r26 (c35→c44)?? And r26 (c44→c17)?? A single row can't go both ways in one loop.
Maybe there are two loops:
Loop 1 (top): r17 (c23,26,29,32,35) + c35 (r20,23) + r26 (c35,38,41,44) + c44?? No, c44 has only one block.
I'm going in circles (pun intended). Let me probe more: click the bottom red (35,14) and the top green (26,48), and observe the diffs. That will reveal the other cycles.

sections.label: ASSISTANT
sections.content:
World model (revised):
- Clicking the upper red piece (26,14) rotates only the upper band row (r26, c17–44, 10-cycle) one step to the left (toward the red piece), with wraparound (c17→c44). The outer loop and the lower band did not move.
- Therefore, the upper red controls the upper band row. Presumably the lower red controls the lower band row (r35), and the green piece controls the outer loop (unverified).
- The targets (26,35) and (35,35) are on the band rows, but the band has no Y block. The Y block is on the outer loop → the outer loop must be able to move/transfer Y. The mechanism is still unclear.
Plan: Investigate the lower red (35,14) and the upper green (26,48), and map out the remaining cycles.

sections.label: TOOL CALL: python
sections.content:
<tool_call>
<function=python>
<parameter=code>
def snap():
    a = ''.join(current_frame.ascii)
    def cell(r,c): return a[r*65+c]
    pos = []
    for c in range(23,36,3): pos.append((17,c))
    for r in range(20,45,3): pos.append((r,23)); pos.append((r,35))
    for c in range(26,35,3): pos.append((44,c))
    for c in range(17,45,3): pos.append((26,c)); pos.append((35,c))
    return {f"{r},{c}": cell(r,c) for r,c in pos}
b1 = snap()
r = action([{'action':'MOUSE','row':35,'col':14}])
a1 = snap()
print("bottom red:", {k:r[k] for k in ('board_changed','done','level_completed','game_over','run_complete')})
print("diff:", {k:(b1[k],a1[k]) for k in b1 if b1[k]!=a1[k]})
b2 = snap()
r = action([{'action':'MOUSE','row':26,'col':48}])
a2 = snap()
print("top green:", {k:r[k] for k in ('board_changed','done','level_completed','game_over','run_complete')})
print("diff:", {k:(b2[k],a2[k]) for k in b2 if b2[k]!=a2[k]})
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
